title: FDA Recalls Generic Zyrtec Made in India Over Ranitidine Contamination Risk
excerpt: Four lots of cetirizine hydrochloride tablets manufactured at a Gujarat plant may contain traces of ranitidine, which could trigger life-threatening allergic reactions in sensitive individuals.
body:
• The FDA announced a voluntary recall of four lots of generic cetirizine hydrochloride tablets (generic Zyrtec) over possible cross-contamination with ranitidine, a drug previously pulled from the U.S. market.
  • Manufacturer Unique Pharmaceutical Laboratories, a division of India-based J.B. Chemicals & Pharmaceuticals Ltd., initiated the recall after a pharmacy technician spotted discolored tablets with red spots.
  • People hypersensitive to ranitidine face a risk of anaphylaxis, though no adverse events have been reported so far.
  • The affected tablets were distributed nationwide by New Jersey-based Rising Pharma Holdings Inc. in 100-count bottles.

The U.S. Food and Drug Administration on Monday announced the recall of a widely used over-the-counter allergy medication after tablets manufactured at an Indian pharmaceutical plant were found to be potentially cross-contaminated with another drug, one that could cause life-threatening reactions in certain consumers.

Four lots of 5-milligram cetirizine hydrochloride tablets—generic versions of the popular antihistamine Zyrtec—are covered by the voluntary recall. The tablets were manufactured by Unique Pharmaceutical Laboratories, a division of J.B. Chemicals & Pharmaceuticals Ltd., based in Panoli, Gujarat, and distributed across the United States by Rising Pharma Holdings Inc. of New Jersey, according to the FDA.

How the Problem Was Discovered

The contamination came to light through an unusually sharp-eyed catch at the pharmacy counter. A pharmacy technician noticed something off while counting tablets before dispensing: some pills bore a “red dot,” while others appeared discolored or had multiple red-colored spots, prompting an investigation by the manufacturer.

Testing revealed the tablets may have been cross-contaminated with ranitidine, a stomach acid reducer once sold under the brand name Zantac. Ranitidine was pulled from the U.S. market in 2020 after regulators found it could contain NDMA, a probable human carcinogen. A reformulated version was approved by the FDA in 2025.

"For consumers with a hypersensitivity to the ingredients in ranitidine, there is a reasonable probability that ingestion of cetirizine tablets contaminated with ranitidine could result in serious adverse events."

— U.S. Food and Drug Administration

The FDA warned that affected consumers could experience anaphylaxis—a rapid, potentially fatal allergic reaction. Symptoms include low blood pressure, difficulty breathing, throat and facial swelling, intense itching, hives, and loss of consciousness.

Affected Products and What To Do

The recall covers cetirizine hydrochloride tablets sold in 100-count high-density polyethylene bottles under National Drug Code 16571-401-10. The four affected lot numbers are GY825029, GY825030, GY825031, and GY825032, all with an expiration date of October 2028, according to the FDA notice. The product was distributed nationwide to wholesalers and retailers.

Unique Pharmaceutical Laboratories said it has not received any reports of adverse events linked to the affected medication. Consumers with questions can contact Rising Pharma Holdings at 1-844-874-7464 between 8 a.m. and 5 p.m. ET, Monday through Friday, or email pv@risingpharma.com.

The FDA urged anyone who may have experienced side effects to report them through the agency’s MedWatch Adverse Event Reporting program.

India’s Generic Drug Pipeline Under Scrutiny

The recall puts a spotlight on quality control at Indian pharmaceutical manufacturing facilities that supply a significant share of the generic drugs consumed in the United States. India is the world’s largest exporter of generic medicines, and Indian-made drugs account for roughly 40 percent of the U.S. generic drug supply, according to industry estimates.

J.B. Chemicals & Pharmaceuticals is a Mumbai-listed company whose Panoli, Gujarat facility has manufactured at least 162 generic drugs for the U.S. market, according to ProPublica’s FDA inspection database. The plant had received a clean Establishment Inspection Report from the FDA in 2020, with no objectionable observations.

For Indian Americans who rely heavily on affordable generic medications, the recall underscores the importance of checking lot numbers and staying informed about FDA safety alerts. Consumers should not stop taking allergy medication without consulting a healthcare provider but should verify whether their specific product is among the recalled lots.

What’s Next

Rising Pharma Holdings has notified distributors and customers of the recall via email. The FDA continues to monitor the situation and has urged consumers to contact their physicians if they have concerns about their medication. The agency’s enforcement database lists the recall status as ongoing.

The incident adds to a growing list of drug recalls in 2026, with the FDA also recently flagging contamination issues with infant formula and garlic powder products. For the pharmaceutical industry, the case is a reminder that even routine generic manufacturing carries quality risks that can cascade across international supply chains.
